We focus our analysis on designs which adhere to the hypothesis of known analytical theory for fixed-priority scheduling. Unlike previous formal approaches, we profit from that theory and build rather simple and tractable formal models based on Timed Automata [l]. Therefore, we are integrating scheduling analysis techniques into the framework of automatic formal verification.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: A rigorous verification of detailed designs for timing requirements is a key aspect of the development process of real-time critical systems. For example, the will to predict schedulability (whether tasks meet their defined deadlines), a typical hard real-time requirement , has encouraged the development of a useful collection of results and tools for run-time scheduling (e.g., [7]). Nevertheless, task schedulability, is not the only deterministic timing requirement that need to be verified. Usually, high level End-to-End timing requirements (requirements established on the system's inputs and outputs, generally involving more than one component) make or break design correctness [6]. Examples of those requirements are: responsiveness (bounds on response times for events), timing requirements for sample and output rates, freshness constraints (bounds on the age of data used in the system), correlation constraints (the maximum time-skew between several inputs used to produce an output) , availability of data or space when asynchronous communication is performed, guarantee on the We focus our proposal on designs which adhere to the assumptions of fixed-priority scheduling theory [7]. Fixedpriority scheduling has been used by a large number of applications in the real-time field and inspired extensions to O.S. standards like POSIX. In particular, we propose an automatic verification technique for concrete architectures featuring: event and time-triggered tasks distributed in a net of processing resources and scheduled by a preemtive fixed-priority technique (e.g., Rate Monotonic [7]); shared memories, queues, circular buffers and signal channels as task connectors; abstract description of tasks code (relevant events do not necessarily occur at the end of them); description of known assumptions about the environment behavior, etc. We aim at checking that complex safety properties hold on non-trivial architectures as the previously mentioned ones. We propose the basis for an efficient automatic formal approach to complement manual reasoning and simulations. In this way, more confidence is gained on the correctness of proposed designs.

div.head: Prior Research
div.p: The verification of real-time systems designs has been considered an interesting application field for automatic space state analysis. Some operational formal notations were adapted to address the processor-sharing phenomena (e.g., preemption of tasks) and some tools were developed (e.g., [5, 3, 21). Unfortunately, dealing with the concepts of elapsed and executed time impacts negatively on the decidability or the tractability of the verification problems. Also, models produced by those techniques are either monolithic or are composed of agents whose behaviors are heavily dependent on each other since they share the same processing resource. This allows us to use known scheduling theory to automatically derive rather simple and non-preemtive formal models from designer's notations. Generality of former approaches prevent authors from using that theory.

We chose Timed Automata (TA) [l] as kernel formalism. TA are finite automata where (dense) time is incorporated by means of clocks. Transitions model event occurrences while clocks serve to measure time elapsed since those event occurrences. Temporal conditions (conditions on clocks values) are associated to transitions and locations to express when transitions may/must be taken. TA are supported by some well established model checking tools (e.g., [4]) which were successfully applied in some application fields such as protocol verification.

div.head: Details of Our Approach
div.p: Some scheduling analysis techniques produce as one of the outcomes the Worst Case Completion Time (WCCT or response time from release instant) of certain code areas. Our technique uses those calculated WCCT together with best case execution times estimates provided by designers to build an abstract model of the system based on TA. In our models neither the scheduler nor tasks priorities are explicitly represented. The translation procedure proposed just leaves their influence on task response times (timing information for the timed automata). That is, each task is modeled by a timed automaton whose transitions are the end of its relevant actions. Expressive power of TA allows the description of temporal conditions which imply that transitions must occur within the best and worst case response times of the corresponding event. Thus, task activities are modeled as running in dedicated processors (maximal parallelism with no preemption). The models produced are conservative. That is, they might have more behaviors than the actual systems but they are safe to verify 'nothing bad happens' properties (safety properties). Usually, designers want to know whether the system may behave in such a way that the analyzed requirement is violated. In our proposal, designers describe a timed automaton which synchronizes with those events which are relevant to the property and evolves to an Error location if an invalidating behavior is present in the system. TA are able to express rather complex timing requirements which involve more than one component. Then, we use known tools to perform reachability analysis (Is Error reachable?) on the parallel composition of the timed automata obtained by the translation procedure with the query automaton. It is important to say that given a query only a subset of components are needed to perform the verification process (i,e,. it does not require the whole model of the system as in previous approaches).

div.head: Empirical Evaluation and Preliminary Results
div.p: We are constructing a tool that given the system's architecture, the context assumptions and the requirement the system must satisfy, produces a TA-model needed to perform the verification. The resultant model would be automatically verified afterwards with tools like KRO-NOS [4]. The preliminary results obtained on built-byhand models were really promissory due to the fact that the method focus on the components which are relevant for the query. That is, the complexity of our approach mainly depends on the number of components involved by the requirement (not in the number of components of the system like in the precedent approaches). Thanks to this remark, we believe that this technique may be useful for real size designs whenever analyzed data and/or control flows involve not too many components.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: This proposal, in some sense, enlarges the applicability of scheduling theory to deal with other kind of requirements. We also show how known scheduling results could be used to reduce the complexity of the models and consequently of their analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first proposal to model preemptive systems using a dense time formalism which does not support time accumulation constraints.
